title: Could Meta fix its glasses privacy issues with an LED redesign?
snippet: The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone? more…
fullText:
The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

Meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

😎The Meta Glasses Black Friday sale has begun!

Meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the company’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

	

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

So this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

title: Hackers Are Using AI to Speed Through Cyberattacks, FBI Warns
snippet: The agency says the Artex tool is helping attackers target organizations worldwide, including banks, government agencies and healthcare providers.
fullText:
An open-source AI tool designed to find security flaws is helping hackers launch cyberattacks. The FBI says hackers are using Artex, an AI-powered security testing tool, to break into organizations worldwide. In an advisory on Friday, the agency said some attacks took less than 3 hours from selecting a target to gaining high-level access to its systems. Attackers have used Artex since at least August against banks, government agencies, technology companies and healthcare providers.

The advisory was issued the same day communications problems prompted a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop and a day after a major Microsoft 365 outage began. Microsoft attributed its disruption to technical problems, and the FAA says it has found no indication of a cyberattack. 

An FBI official told ABC News⁠ that Artex doesn’t appear to be connected to either incident or to other recent disruptions, including banking outages involving JPMorgan Chase.

			

More from CNET

The warning adds to concerns about the security risks posed by AI agents, which can carry out tasks with little human supervision.

Artex automates security tests that organizations use to uncover weaknesses. According to Microsoft’s analysis, its agents can examine defenses, exploit flaws and extract data. Attackers can use that automation to try several ways into a network simultaneously.

The FBI cited attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed the personal information of approximately 67,000 people. Microsoft warns that attackers breached over 2,250 organizations’ Microsoft 365 systems in a separate campaign, using stolen ConnectWise backup credentials alongside the Artex tool.

Because customers had already authorized the backup software, attackers could use its access without logging in as an individual user. Microsoft cautioned that a successful sign-in doesn’t necessarily mean data was accessed or stolen. The automated attacks could trigger security alerts, but their speed left defenders little time to respond.

This FBI Cyber advisory on ARTEX was released last Friday, 11/13. It is not a new announcement, and the FBI has not issued any additional warning since. The guidance in the advisory remains current.

We released this advisory last week because as we head to the end of the year,…

— FBI (@FBI) November 17, 2026

Amazon Web Services’ Nov. 13 research described another scheme: Stealing credentials for AI services, and then using that access to hunt for more credentials at someone else’s expense. Amazon Threat Intelligence uncovered the activity through decoy systems posing as AI services. It linked the campaigns to Artex with moderate confidence but couldn’t independently verify results the agents reported on systems outside its monitoring.

Amazon said the attacks relied on default passwords, exposed login details and outdated software, all of which hackers can find and exploit faster with AI.

Artex’s developer removed the original GitHub repository in October after reports of abuse, but copies remain available, the FBI said. The agency recommends limiting access to sensitive systems, reviewing software permissions, replacing exposed credentials, and monitoring unusual account activity or large data transfers.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Nelson Aguilar
						

						

											

								

											With more than a decade of experience, Nelson covers Apple and Google and writes about iPhone and Android features, privacy and security settings, and more.

title: macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more
snippet: Last month, Apple announced its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents. With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this. more…
fullText:
Last month, Apple announced its plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

What’s changing in macOS 27.3

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

Accessibility: Intended specifically for assistive technologies, with permissions handled through an entitlement process.

System and App Protection Override: A new category for apps that need to bypass certain macOS protections to control other apps or perform automated tasks.

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Full Disk Access isn’t going away

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates. 

For developers

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
snippet: Nvidia's interim CEO reaffirmed its open source AI strategy and plans to acquire Hugging Face, despite Jensen Huang's sudden departure.
fullText:
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

“At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months. 

Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history.

The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.”

So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call.

“Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face.

Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.”

“That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said. 

Correction: Due to a typo, an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the number of developers served by Hugging Face; it is 18 million, not 118 million.

title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
snippet: Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals, including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
fullText:
The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns.

Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel.

“Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”

OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology.

Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.”

“I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.”

Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people, including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.”

“I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
snippet: Nvidia began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” | Image: Nvidia This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control. It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand i … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control.

It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off.

“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.”

Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever.

Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents.

Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.

“Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent.

Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs.

Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales.

Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC.

So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength.

But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.

“While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.”

There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.

According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models.

But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly.

“It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.”

Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says.

That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up.

Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents.

That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028.

“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said.

Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook.

For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going.

title: Apple’s Siri AI smart glasses are reportedly launching next year, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long awaited smart glasses, akin to Meta Ray-Bans but tailored to Siri AI and the Apple ecosystem, are almost here. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the product should be introduced at the next WWDC, and they should be on the market by the end of the year. Here’s what to expect.

First and foremost, Apple wants to rely on its deep app ecosystem to give its glasses a boost. While companies like Meta are undeniably leading in the agentic AI assistant game, the third party app integration just isn’t quite there.

Starting with iOS 27.3 beta, Apple is finally laying the groundwork for proper third party app integration within Siri, rather than just Siri Shortcuts. By the time the glasses release at the end of next year, there should be a plethora of third-party integrations to utilize.

That said, the glasses themselves won’t run apps directly. Everything will rely on a nearby iPhone, per Gurman. The glasses will still have Wi-Fi for apps to function if an iPhone isn’t nearby, but these will largely serve as an iPhone accessory.

According to the report, Apple’s glasses will likely be slightly thinner than a pair of Meta Ray-Bans:

In terms of industrial design, internal prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta’s second-generation Ray-Ban glasses. At least on some test units, the cameras are housed in oval-shaped openings that sit flush with the frame — rather than protruding from it. There’s also a light on the front that shows when the glasses are in use or charging. Apple has been experimenting with other features on the front of the glasses related to privacy.

Lastly, a big focus of these glasses is the audio quality. According to Bloomberg, engineers are describing the audio quality as “industry-leading.”

title: The UGREEN HomeAgent is a ‘local-first’ way to make your smart home even smarter
snippet: Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home. more…
fullText:
Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

The UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

At the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

	

UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

Meanwhile, the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro is a pan-tilt-zoom camera meant to be used inside to capture events in an entire room. It features 4K imaging, 360-degree pan and 160-degree vertical tilt while supporting up to 8x digital zoom, motion tracking, and even baby-cry detection. It also has a physical shutter for your privacy.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

You can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.

title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro debuts globally with sub-mm bezels, privacy display, rear display, and 200MP Leica cameras
snippet: Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

If you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a new phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

During the launch presentation, Xiaomi emphasized that its new privacy display wasn’t just a copy of “other privacy displays.” Rather, they created an entirely new subpixel layout called HyperRGB 2.0 that delivers far higher resolution and brightness output than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. You can also enable and disable the privacy display feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series with a click of the new AI button on the left side of the phone. Functionally, Xiaomi’s privacy display looks nearly identical to Samsung’s, including the ability to have specific apps use it.

Both models feature identical specs, including the privacy display and cameras, with the exception of the screen size, battery capacity, and charging speed. Here are the differences:

	

Spec

Xiaomi 18 Pro

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max

Display size

6.4-inches

6.9-inches

Battery capacity

6,000mAh

7,050mAh

Charging speed

90W wired, 50W wireless

100W wired, 50W wireless

The 120Hz LTPO display is bordered by a 0.99mm bezel, the smallest in the industry so far, 4,000-nit peak brightness, and TÜV Rheinland Triple Eye Care Certification, including a 2160Hz PWM dimming rate. Inside the phone is a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor with a 3D IceLoop cooling system, and each model’s silicon-carbon battery includes 28% silicon content.

On the back is a pair of 200MP cameras, including a 1/1.28-inch main sensor and a 1/1.56-inch periscope telephoto sensor. These are massive sensors, especially compared to the 1/3.94″ and 1/2.52″ telephoto sensors in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Despite their size, Xiaomi packs them onto the back in an island with fully flat glass — no protruding camera lenses!

That island on the back isn’t just for cameras, though. It also packs in a 120Hz LTPO M11 OLED panel with 4,000-nit peak brightness for ultra-high-quality selfies and group shots, plus support for notifications and apps. Xiaomi created a new GenAI Apps feature that lets you create your own apps on the back display, plus official support for several popular apps like Google Maps, Spotify, and more.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series ships with HyperOS 4 (Android 17) and includes 3 months of Google AI Pro, plus 5TB of Google Cloud storage. The Xiaomi 18 Pro retails for €1399 for the model with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, or €1599 for 12GB/512GB. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at €1599 for 12GB/256GB, €1799 for 12GB/512GB, and a 16GB/1TB model will be available soon for €2099.

Some retailers also sell a bundle that includes the Official silicone magnetic case, which usually retails for €39, as well as the Magnetic Remote Stand, which retails for €69. That remote stand functions as a MagSafe-style stand and remote, giving you camera shutter functionality and a scrolling feature.

title: Apple provides a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health
snippet: A growing number of people are asking AI chatbots about their health issues, raising two major concerns: safety and privacy. Apple is now offering a safer way to do this through an Apple Health AI Usage Study. This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots … more…
fullText:
A growing number of people are asking AI chatbots about their health issues, raising two major concerns: safety and privacy. Apple is now offering a safer way to do this through an Apple Health AI Usage Study.

This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots …

Apple Health AI Usage Study

Apple launched its Research app back in 2019 with the goal of allowing customers to help universities and medical institutions with health studies. You typically agree to share certain anonymized information from the Apple Health app in order to provide data that can advance medical research. You may also be asked to complete questionnaires.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is one of these, but it works in a somewhat different way. You’ll still be invited to share some of your health data, but will also be able to ask an AI system questions about your health.

Three key assurances

When you ask health questions of a typical AI chatbot, you don’t know how reliable those answers may be or what will happen to your data. Apple study offers three assurances:

Authoritative sources

Not used for AI training

No retention of questions or answers

Authoritative sources

Apple says that answers will be generated by the same platform used by healthcare professionals.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. 

The answers provided to you will include links to peer-reviewed clinical citations.

Your data won’t be used for AI training

As you’d expect from Apple, there are strong privacy protections, including the assurance that your data will not be used to train AI models.

The study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information.

No retention of questions or answers

CNET reports on Apple’s assurance that none of your chats will be retained.

OpenEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

How to get access

Access to the study is currently limited to users in the US by downloading the app. If you try it, please do share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
snippet: Nvidia's interim CEO says the company is done selling chips to China. How much will that cost?
fullText:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. 

Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.

The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”

Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.

Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.

In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.

Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.

That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.

If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

title: Here’s how Google’s Android XR glasses are handling the camera & privacy
snippet: Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance. more…
fullText:
Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

To quickly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an issue of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

	

It starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Users also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

The camera on a pair of Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear glasses

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

One of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

Continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

Another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google said that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes. 

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google says it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:

Responsible use requirements: Before using intelligent eyewear, users must agree not to record others without permission, not to record in sensitive places, and not to cover the recording indicator light. Not following these requirements is a violation of the Google Terms of Service, and a user’s ability to use the glasses may be disabled.

Google Shopping and Google Ads: Policies ban the sale and advertising of stickers or accessories designed to hide recording lights.

Google Play: Policies prohibit apps from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification, and from changing the behavior of the outer indicator light.

YouTube: Policies prohibit content that depicts things like harassment and unwanted sexualization. Any video uploaded to YouTube — whether it’s recorded on a phone, a camera, or glasses — has to follow these policies, and videos that don’t are removed.

Account restrictions: Activating an intelligent eyewear device requires an 18+ Google account.

9to5Google’s Take

For the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.” 

What do you think?

title: Material 3 Expressive adds scrolling time picker, AI Studio upgrades Android app creation
snippet: Google has given the time picker component a Material 3 Expressive redesign, while adding a new scrolling variant. Meanwhile, Google AI Studio is boosting its Android app development experience. more…
fullText:
Google has given the time picker component a Material 3 Expressive redesign, while adding a new scrolling variant. Meanwhile, Google AI Studio is boosting its Android app development experience.

Compared to Material 3, the updated M3 Expressive input and dial time pickers drop the “Select time” hint in the top-right corner, while the AM and PM buttons now benefit from expressive shape, color, and behavior. The hour and minute fields, as well as the dial selector, feature higher contrast.

Old vs. new (input & dial)

The big addition today is the scroll time picker. Instead of using the keyboard or analog clock to pick the time, you can just vertically scroll when setting an alarm or scheduling an event. 

	

The Material Design team says this “compact way to select time” is “best placed inline with other content.” A keyboard icon lets you switch to the input time picker. 

Use scroll time pickers instead of dial pickers when you want people to see surrounding content.

You can see various examples below:

Google today also introduced scroll fields to select different units of measurement, like distance, weight, or temperature. In a health app, they can be used for water, calories, and more.

In other related developments, building an Android app in Google AI Studio got an upgrade today. The updates include:

Full-stack persistence and sign-in: Automatically provision a Cloud Firestore database with Security Rules and Google Sign-In so user data syncs across sessions and devices.

Secure Gemini API calls: Call Gemini models from your Android app without exposing API keys in your APK, protected by Firebase AI Logic and Firebase App Check.

Personal Google Play publishing: Ship Android apps directly to your personal Google Play library with a standard Google account and install them on your phone in clicks.

Faster, high-definition emulator with audio: Spin up Android emulators with lower latency, toggle HD video streaming, and test real-time audio output directly in your browser.

One-click screenshot to agent: Capture a live frame from the running emulator with a single click and attach it to your prompt to guide visual UI edits.

Custom fonts and Android CLI integration: Style Jetpack Compose UIs with custom typography, backed under the hood by the official Android CLI for reliable project scaffolding and builds.

title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
snippet: Gemini's Task mode can help users coordinate calls, log into websites, and even make purchases on the user's behalf.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

11:02 AM PST · November 17, 2026

Image Credits:Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.

How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.

In a blog post, Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.

Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. 

Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

Some countries excluded

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries. 

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Brazil

South Korea

The UK

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After releasing a $28 leak sensor earlier this year that conveniently runs off a battery for two years, Shelly is announcing an accompanying smart valve you can install on your home’s main water line to automatically turn off the flow when one of those sensors detects a problem. The Shelly Neo Smart Water Valve is available now through the company’s online store for $499.99, plus the cost of installation if you don’t trust your plumbing skills. It’s not a cheap solution, but it’s cheaper than the fallout of a leak turning into a disaster.

The Neo Smart Water Valve is designed to be installed on a standard US 1-inch thread connection (the company plans to launch additional size options next year) and is made from brass so it’s safe to use on plumbing carrying drinking water. It has an IPX7 waterproof rating so the valve will keep working if flooding means it ends up submerged. However, the valve lacks a battery of its own and requires a connection to a power source through an included USB adapter cable. Connecting it to a waterproof power bank instead of an outlet may be the best approach to ensure it still works during a power outage.

The smart valve connects to other devices over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and is designed to integrate into existing smart home setups using webhooks, MQTT, or scripting for advanced users. In addition to shutting off the flow of water into your home in about 12 seconds, the valve also features an ultrasonic measurement system that tracks pressure, flow rate, your home’s consumption, and even the temperature of the water. Through the Shelly app, you can monitor all of that data in order to spot unusual usage patterns that could indicate a wasteful leak, or ensure the pressure doesn’t get high enough to damage pipes or appliances.

title: New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training
snippet: Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.” more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”

Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options. 

	

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

	

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public. 

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

title: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents
snippet: With a team of just seven, Unsiloed AI plans to compete with tech giants and specialized startups in the crowded AI document-processing market.
fullText:
As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology.

Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated.

Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work.

Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value.

“The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”

Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology.

Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors.

Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document.

“In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.”

The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts.

Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified.

Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts.

Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way.

Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology.

title: British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts
snippet: Two British hackers face lengthy prison sentences for hacks that broke into the Grand Theft Auto gamemaker and for stealing millions in crypto.
fullText:
Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency.

Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays. 

Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial.

U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions.

Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider. These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks.

Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase, DoorDash, Mailchimp, and Nvidia.

By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case.

title: Amid AI Industry Chaos, Microsoft and OpenAI Drop New Models for Coding and Work
snippet: While Nvidia and Anthropic are under the spotlight, OpenAI and Microsoft dropped several new models this week.
fullText:
It has been a wild week for AI, and it’s only Wednesday. Aside from outages, cheating scandals and upcoming IPOs, there are several new models available now. Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models.

First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription. 

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program, which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace.

			

More from CNET

Next, OpenAI: The ChatGPT maker dropped two new model variants of its flagship model, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the big model — it costs the most and uses the most firepower to handle complex tasks — and Sol is the “everyday” version. Both models beat their sibling models in OpenAI’s benchmarking. These are available to paying subscribers in ChatGPT and Codex globally now. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

The AI elephant in the room

While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify.

And let’s not forget about Anthropic, the Claude maker plans to become a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO slated for Thursday. Anthropic’s reportedly seeking an opening price of $78 per share, for a total valuation of $1.4 trillion — narrowly beating the other largest-ever IPO earlier this year, Elon’s Musk mega-conglomerate, SpaceX (including now SpaceXSI, because President Trump said so).

The Nvidia scandal caused a drastic 14% dip in its stock price during its first week and wiped out $1 trillion in the company’s value, but Anthropic investors don’t seem to be worried. At least, not publicly.

If nothing else, Anthropic’s IPO and the new models from OpenAI and Microsoft are stark reminders that the tech industry is nowhere near ready to slow down on AI. Even as financial, environmental and legal concerns mount — and arguably hit a fever pitch during the midterm elections — Big Tech is plowing ahead with generative AI.

title: Disney Imagineers Have Built AI-Powered ‘Star Wars’ Alien Audio-Animatronics With AWS
snippet: Semi-exclusive: Three original Anzellan characters with distinct personalities will interact with guests in Disney parks.
fullText:
Disney is celebrating 75 years of its Imagineers, who have been amusing and delighting guests with audio-animatronic characters since talking parrots debuted in the Enchanted Tiki Room at Disneyland. But today, new robotic characters are being powered up with artificial intelligence.

In partnership with Amazon Web Services, AI has helped Walt Disney Imagineering create three new Anzellan animatronics that will live bring a Disney theme park retail space to life, presumably in Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge. 

Anzellans are a race of tiny humanoid creatures that repair droids and starships in the Star Wars universe. They include Babu Frik in Star Wars: Episode IX — The Rise of Skywalker and the droidsmiths introduced in season 3 of The Mandalorian. The droidsmiths take on larger roles in The Mandalorian and Grogu, helping Baby Yoda rescue Din Djarin from the Hutts.

			

More from CNET

The new Anzellan animatronics built by Disney Imagineers use AWS cloud and AI capabilities in order to “understand the scene around them,” Kyle Laughlin, SVP of Walt Disney Imagineering R&D and Technology and Engineering, tells me.

“If you imagine walking into an experiential retail store, you now will be greeted not by a pre-scripted animation or interaction, but a totally personalized experience where each of these Anzellans [has] their own personalities,” Laughlin says, adding that they’ll be attuned to “how many people are in the room, the ages of people, the general size and type of guest.”

The animatronic aliens will be able to interact with guests, right down to commenting on people who are wearing a birthday button or even a certain Star Wars T-shirt. Speaking with these animatronics will give guests the same experience they would have when meeting a character walking around the park, Laughlin adds. They also play off each other and react to what each other are doing, with no one controlling them behind the scenes.

The three audio-animatronic prototypes, which will make their first appearance during AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas on Nov. 30 before moving into one of the Disney Parks, are named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a.

They’re original characters created just for this project in partnership with Lucasfilm and the filmmakers, and they all have their own personalities devised by the Imagineers. Vilo is the boss, Kado is the droidsmith mechanic who wants to be the center of attention and Jibu, though Kado’s twin, is the shy one. The animatronics speak a mix of English (or Galactic Basic in-universe) and Anzellan, as they do in the Star Wars movies and TV series, and have hundreds of thousands of prerecorded lines of dialogue to draw from when talking to guests and each other.

The three audio-animatronic Anzellans are original characters named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a.Disney

Samira Panah Bakhtiar, AWS general manager of Telco, Media & Entertainment, Games, Advertising and Sports, tells me this is “one of the most delightful examples” of physical AI.

“When you talk about physical AI, it’s AI that perceives, it reasons and it acts in the real world,” she says. “It’s not just AI on a screen.”

Bakhtiar says Disney was able to use both AWS cloud computing and AI tools to “get from idea to implementation several magnitudes faster than they would have otherwise,” with Laughlin specifying it took “mere months.”

Imagineers used an AWS coding agent called Kiro that built their creative briefs into software, which was then reviewed by humans. Imagineers also used the Amazon Bedrock fully managed AI service, which allows them to choose between all the biggest AI models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.

“We’re providing Amazon Bedrock to the Imagineering team to be able to leverage the right models that they need at the right time to be able to really enhance those character experiences,” Bakhtiar tells me. “From multimodal models that focus on voice to world models, to large language models. The point is that they are able to get the right tool at the right time and then do so in a way that’s secure, resilient, performant and globally available.”

Bakhtiar says AWS is continuing to work with Disney, though the next project is under wraps.

“The future of entertainment is going to be highly personalized,” she says. “It’s going to be multidimensional, and it’s going to be more interactive than ever. And I think this is an incredible example of that coming to life.”

Disney had previously teamed up with Nvidia on robotics and AI to bring a robot version of fan-favorite Frozen character Olaf to life so he can wander around Disneyland Paris and Hong Kong Disneyland, and is also now exploring robots paired with AI that could guide guests throughout Disneyland parking lots.

“You can imagine an entire franchise of characters working and interacting with one another,” says Laughlin. “We’ve done a number of things in the Star Wars universe. We’re just getting started in Frozen, and we have a wealth of IP that we can mine to bring those characters to our guests as fast as possible.”

She holds degrees in law and communications, and currently writes news, analysis and features for CNET across the topics of electric vehicles, broadband networks, mobile devices, big tech, artificial intelligence, home technology and entertainment. title: Google AI Mode rolling out temporary threads
snippet: Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small update to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small update to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

Like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

To launch, tap the new pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”

	

This is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now quickly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

title: Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits
snippet: iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know. 

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

Siri AI

Photo tools: Clean Up, Extend, Spatial Reframing, and Image Playground

AFM Cloud and Cloud Pro models in Shortcuts

Third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit. 

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

title: Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]
snippet: Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand. Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases. more…
fullText:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.
