title: Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway
snippet: The most fascinating and frustrating device I’ve used in a long time pushes at the edges of where headsets are heading, and glasses are evolving.
fullText:
Scott Stein/CNET		

	

		

					

	7.0

	
					

			

	

		

			

				Pros & Cons			

			

			

							

					
						Very portable					
				

							

					
						Runs multiple Android apps at once on a virtual display					
				

							

					
						Works as display glasses for other devices via USB-C cable					
				

							

					
						Big-for-glasses viewing area, crisp display					
				

							

					
						Battery lasts longer than most VR headsets					
				

							

					
						Onboard Gemini can see apps and the world around you					
				

					

			

							

					
						Touchpad and hand tracking inputs work but often feel limiting and awkward					
				

							

					
						Glasses field of view still less than VR, restricting immersive experiences					
				

							

					
						No VR controller support					
				

							

					
						Processor puck can get hot when venting air					
				

							

					
						Android XR still doesn't have many truly unique apps yet					
				

							

					
						Need separate wireless keyboard to properly type on the go					
				

					

	

		

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

There are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

		

			

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

Emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Xreal Aura glasses perched on top of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR. Look at the size difference!Scott Stein/CNET

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

The Xreal Aura in its included carry case. This thing packs small.Scott Stein/CNET

What it is: A little AR glasses kit

Android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

The Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D. 

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing. 

Xreal Aura in its carrying case, next to a separately-sold Xreal game controller (for size).Scott Stein/CNET

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

The Xreal Aura glasses have three cameras that handle tracking and visual AI.Scott Stein/CNET

The displays: The good and the bad

The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a big movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view). 

When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

The display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

A selfie of me wearing the Xreal Aura.Scott Stein/CNET

A whole lot of Android on my face

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

Hand tracking and windowed apps sometimes feel VR-familiar.Scott Stein/CNET

Controls and Android XR take a lot of getting used to

The whole Aura interface feels new-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides. 

You can use the puck as a trackpad, scrolling and tapping.Scott Stein/CNET

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted. 

The side of the puck, where the fingerprint sensor power button is.Scott Stein/CNET

The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

Watching some MacGruber on YouTube.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

Android XR apps are still a mixed bag

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, captured in-glasses. Keep in mind, this looks better than my experience because you can’t see how limited the field of view is.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely. 

Navigating Coney Island in 3D Google Maps with my hands.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

Sock Puppet Superstar is a hoot. It works with hand tracking.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

Cubism in the glasses: It looks overlaid in the real world. Hand tracking isn’t always accurate enough, though.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

The refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I said before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

Xreal’s Aura glasses on their own are familiar-looking (lens inserts are in).Scott Stein/CNET

How is this different from Xreal’s other glasses (and Google smart glasses)

Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or launches live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

Speakers are embedded in the arms, pumping out audio that sounds as good as Xreal’s other glasses. Fine for games and movies, but you might prefer earbuds for isolation and privacy.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

Sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

Real-life shot of me working at breakfast, writing on the Xreal Aura with a separately sold wireless keyboard.Scott Stein/CNET

Can I work in it? Kind of!

I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

Xreal’s own folding keyboard responds well. The processor puck is the trackpad.Scott Stein/CNET

But what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask. 

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

Connecting the new iPad Mini to the Aura, which makes a second display for the iPad. But so many cables!Scott Stein/CNET

It connects to almost everything, though (with a USB-C cable)

Connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

Right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

Behold: Playing Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, connected to the Xreal Aura, while also watching Bridget Carey’s latest One More Thing. (My hands are holding Joy-Cons you can’t see).Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

Whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Alas, this is how you need to connect the Switch 2.Scott Stein/CNET

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort. 

The glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Circle to Search recognized Bridget Carey’s face on YouTube.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

Gemini seeing everything is wild

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

It’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

I got it to Gemini search Ocarina of Time while I was playing.Screenshot by Scott Stein/CNET

This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured. 

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Where the Xreal Aura processor puck wants to live: clipped to your pants.Scott Stein/CNET

Battery life is surprisingly good, but mind those venting fans

Xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

A bridge to a new wave of odd tweener glasses

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually? 

Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close. 

The Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

iPhone Duo, because it offers a much larger inside display, means theres all tons of new use cases that you wouldn’t normally come across with your iPhone. Of course, one of them is the fact that you might want to prop up your iPhone Duo to watch a video on the larger display.

A couple weeks ago, I wrote about one accessory that solves the kickstand problem. That said, what if you want to charge and prop up your phone at the same time?

On iPhone Duo, the charging port is located on the bottom of the device, so it isn’t really possible to charge and have your phone standing up at the same time, unless you want to use it upside down. However, that creates a new problem: button placement.

In recent weeks, I’ve been trying out ESR’s MagSafe puck with a built in kickstand. It supports Qi2 25W charging, and also offers active cooling.

While this accessory isn’t exclusively useful for iPhone Duo, it’s great on iPhone Duo for three reasons:

The kickstand allows you to prop up your phone for content

Active cooling keeps your iPhone Duo cooler, which can be an issue at times

You can take advantage of MagSafe to charge your phone while watching your video, without worrying about the bottom charge port

If you aren’t using this with an iPhone Duo, it’s still an incredible charger. It can fast charge an iPhone 18 Pro to 50% in just 25 minutes.

If you’d like to pick up one of the ESR MagSafe chargers, you can get one in white, black, or burgundy. White and Black are available for $36.99 on Amazon, while Burgundy is available for $42.99 on Amazon.

title: Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard
snippet: Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact. Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose. more…
fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Highlights

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

The story

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Download the app

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.

title: Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]
snippet: The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included. more…
fullText:
The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

Fitbit Edge Review: Too much and too little at the same time

The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

More but simultaneously less

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

What it’s like to use

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

When the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”

With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

Who is this for?

The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

title: ‘Hey Gemini’ hotword debuts on Android XR glasses
snippet: Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start. more…
fullText:
Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start.

Around a decade after “Hey Google” made its debut, Google is introducing its first new always-listening hotword. “Hey Gemini” makes its debut on Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses powered by Android XR, with wearers able to use that hotword in place of “Hey Google.”

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

This is a move that doesn’t come as a huge surprise. If anything, it’s perhaps a bit overdue.

The move from Assistant to Gemini would have been the expected place for Google to make this change, but it’s one that many will certainly welcome. While the hotword you use really won’t matter much at the end of the day, “Hey Google” has been recognized by many to not roll of the tongue very nicely. It’s a phrase that’s easy to stumble over, where “Hey Gemini” is a bit smoother. 

	

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.

title: Gemini skills add file support and sharing ahead of Gems deprecation
snippet: Ahead of the Gems shutdown that starts rolling out tomorrow, Google is adding two key features to Gemini skills. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the Gems shutdown that starts rolling out tomorrow, Google is adding two key features to Gemini skills.

These “reusable, custom instructions” now support files from your device, Google Drive, Gemini Notebook, and Google Photos that can be used as context. You can upload files, up to 100 MB, when you create a skill.

Gemini will “reference these files every time the skill runs in chats and tasks.” Files from Drive and Notebooks will “update in real time so your skill always works from the latest version.” 

Meanwhile, skills can now be shared. Go to the Gemini app’s Customize > Skills page on the web to grant View or Edit permissions. Recipients will receive an email and can review the skill before adding it.

	

Use cases for these new capabilities include:

A marketing team can share a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive.

A team lead can share an onboarding skill grounded in the team handbook.

A teacher can share a lesson-planning skill built on a notebook containing their curriculum.

File support and sharing for Gemini skills are rolling out over the coming weeks for everyone: “Available to all Google Workspace customers and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: New iPhone Duo orders now deliver a month earlier than before
snippet: Interested in getting an iPhone Duo before Christmas? You might be in luck, as Apple’s online store delivery estimates just got pulled forward by a full month, with December delivery now expected. more…
fullText:
Interested in getting an iPhone Duo before Christmas? You might be in luck, as Apple’s online store delivery estimates just got pulled forward by a full month, with December delivery now expected.

iPhone Duo now estimated to deliver in mid-December for new orders from Apple

Apple seems to be finding success in ramping up its iPhone Duo production.

Within minutes of iPhone Duo pre-orders opening on October 16, delivery estimates quickly slipped into November, then December, and after about a half hour of orders, the earliest you could get an iPhone Duo was late January.

Apple did deliver some Duo units earlier than the initial estimates. But the late January timeframe remained in place for all new iPhone Duo orders until now.

But as spotted by Max Weinbach, new iPhone Duo orders from Apple just got bumped up by about a month. Now, delivery estimates are showing December 16-23 for customers in the US and elsewhere.

This is a great indicator that Apple has been able to accelerate production. It’s also likely that there was a slowdown in orders due to the late January estimate putting off prospective buyers, thus making it easier for the company to catch up on backorders.

title: Apple’s leadership overhaul continues with new Apple Pay and Wallet chief
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple lifer Corey Fugman will replace Jennifer Bailey as the head of the Apple Pay and Wallet division. Here are the details.

Apple names Jennifer Bailey’s successor

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Jennifer Bailey, Apple’s head of Apple Pay and Wallet, who had led Apple Pay since its launch in 2014, would retire in October.

At the time, Apple’s services boss Eddy Cue said internally that the company would announce its succession plan before her transition at the end of October, and that she would “continue to be available to support the transition in an advisory role.”

October came and went without any public announcement on that front. Today, however, Bloomberg reported that Apple has tapped Corey Fugman, “a 26-year company veteran as the new head of its payment service and digital wallet unit.”

According to his LinkedIn profile, Fugman joined Apple in September 2000 as Merchandising Manager for Apple Retail and has held several leadership positions since then, including overseeing Apple Card and Apple Cash from 2019 to 2021.

Most recently, he served as Senior Director of Apple Pay and Wallet, a position he has held since November 2021.

Here’s Bloomberg:

With the new job, Fugman inherits a crucial tap-to-pay business, which is estimated to generate billions of dollars a year. It handles tens of billions of transactions annually across more than 90 markets, with Apple taking a percentage.

The division also includes the Apple Card, which is transitioning from a partnership with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to JPMorgan Chase & Co. Fugman has been highly involved with the shift to Chase, which is still ongoing, the people said.

The report notes that Fugman will report to Cue, and reaffirms that Bailey “will remain a consultant in the coming months,” echoing Cue’s earlier comments about her role in the transition.

Finally, Bloomberg adds that while Apple has undergone several leadership changes in recent months, including John Ternus replacing Tim Cook as CEO, Cue’s responsibilities have expanded considerably.

In addition to overseeing services such as Apple TV, Apple Music, Maps, and iCloud, Cue has recently taken charge of the App Store and Health following Jeff Williams’ departure as Chief Operating Officer and Phil Schiller’s decision to step down from overseeing the App Store.

title: I’ve Used VSCO’s Lightroom Rival Desktop Editor and It’s Great for Creatives
snippet: VSCO might be popular for iPhone photography, but its Studio Pro has rival Adobe firmly in its sights.
fullText:
VSCO is best known these days for its iPhone and Android editing app that makes pics look all cool and analog. But the company is launching its first stand-alone desktop photo editor for Mac, called VSCO Studio Pro, bringing its famous filmic presets—and a wealth of editing tools. I’ve used it, and while it’s not yet my sole image-editing solution, it’s great for getting those dreamy vintage vibes out of your photos. 

The desktop app will be immediately familiar to any photographer who’s spent any time in Lightroom or Capture One. There are exposure, contrast, highlight, and shadow sliders along with color sliders for white balance or individual color adjustments. It’s par for the course for any raw image editor. 

VSCO’s wide range of color presets has always been where it shines the brightest. Numbering just north of 200, Studio Pro packs in all the presets, from color classics like the company’s A1-10 range to a wealth of black-and-white options and a host of presets designed to emulate real film stocks like Kodak Gold or Fuji Velvia. VSCO says these are modeled on real scans of these film stocks to make them as authentic as possible.

			

More from CNET

VSCO Studio Pro editor includes presets similar to its beloved ones for Lightroom.Screenshot by Andrew Lanxon/CNET

It’s the presets that I love the most in VSCO’s app. Years ago, the company sold its presets as a downloadable Lightroom preset pack, which I have used in my photography workflow almost daily for the past 13 years, and their look is identical here. While it hasn’t sold the Lightroom preset pack in about a decade, VSCO’s Studio Pro app finally lets photographers achieve those same looks in desktop editing. 

With Studio Pro, VSCO clearly has its sights on Lightroom. While Adobe is increasingly filling its services with various generative AI tools that radically alter your image’s content, VSCO is taking a more stripped-back approach that focuses on the creative side of color and exposure adjustments. 

It’s still quite bare-bones at launch, with several features I need for my own photography missing, like masking. I can’t make selective edits to my images—like using a gradient to tone down the highlights only in the sky. Apparently this is coming soon, as are bloom and halation tools, which are already in the app, but grayed out with a “soon” marker next to them. Ditto the spot removal tool for cleaning up dust or sensor spots. 

Studio Pro’s gallery view. There’s not much in the way of cataloging or organizing right now.Screenshot by Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The big thing for me, though, comes down to cataloging and archiving of my images. I have several terabytes of images cataloged in my Lightroom library, available to edit on any device I sign in on — including phone, tablet or desktop. While VSCO will have some basic organization options within the Studio Pro app (grouping images into “Projects”—again, coming soon), it’s not as full-featured as Lightroom’s archiving system. I worry that once I’m working with thousands of images across multiple photoshoots, things will quickly become cluttered and difficult to navigate. Time will tell. 

I don’t imagine VSCO’s app will necessarily be the first choice for working pros who need strict cataloging, backups and remote access. I count myself in that category, and for me Lightroom’s cloud storage remains the biggest reason to stay with Adobe, while others swear by Capture One for its Sessions-based filing system and its tethered shooting workflow. 

VSCO is better known for its mobile editing app, which includes the same presets and many of the same tools. It’s also included in the Pro subscription.Screenshot by Andrew Lanxon/CNET

By contrast, I see VSCO Studio Pro appealing more to enthusiast photographers who want to efficiently add real creative flair to their images and don’t necessarily want to spend on the commercial tools, cloud storage, or AI options offered by Adobe. 

The app is available today on MacOS (no word on Windows yet) and is available to VSCO Pro subscribers for $70 per year, which includes the Pro tools on the mobile apps, too. By comparison, Adobe Lightroom for desktop and mobile comes in at around $140 per year, which also includes 1TB of cloud storage.

title: Pixel 11 Pro’s HiLight feature also now works on WhatsApp messages
snippet: After being barebones at launch, Google is improving on Pixel 11 Pro’s Hilight feature with message support, now including WhatsApp. more…
fullText:
After being barebones at launch, Google is improving on Pixel 11 Pro’s Hilight feature with message support, now including WhatsApp.

As a part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop that was released this week, Google Messages added support for HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro series. As we reported back in September when Google started beta testing the functionality, users can select a contact and enable a specific color light for phone calls and/or messages.

	

Google’s announcement only officially introduced support for the Google Messages app but, as it turns out, WhatsApp is also supported.

Shenaz Zack, Senior Director of Product Management over Pixel, confirmed through a brief video on Twitter/X that WhatsApp messages can also now activate HiLight. This isn’t a huge surprise given WhatsApp calls have been supported since day one, but it’s a nice addition for the many users who prefer WhatsApp over SMS/RCS.

	

HiLight already worked with WhatsApp calls and now, it works with WhatsApp messages, too, doing the heavy lifting so my favorites get the VIP attention 😄 pic.twitter.com/ouLROk1FeF

Android 17 QPR2 enables the update, and it’s rolling out now to all Pixel 11 Pro devices.

title: Disney+ and Hulu’s ‘fully unified’ app is coming next month
snippet: Disney has announced a major milestone coming next month in its plans to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon. more…
fullText:
Disney has announced a major milestone coming next month in its plans to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon.

Disney+ app will fully integrate all Hulu features starting in December

Today Disney reported its quarterly earnings and gave an update on plans to merge Disney+ and Hulu into one app.

Here’s what the company said:

Our app unification of Disney+ and Hulu is nearly complete. Beginning this December, subscribers will have a fully unified experience on Disney+, including live TV and select premium add-ons, creating a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises.

Live TV and premium add-ons were the final Hulu features that hadn’t yet been imported to the Disney+ app. But by adding those capabilities into Disney+, the app unification will be “complete.”

	

Disney hasn’t said how quickly the Hulu app will be discontinued. But it likely won’t happen until sometime in 2027 at the earliest. The company will want to provide abundant transition time and not risk upsetting its paying subscribers.

The ultimate goal of unifying everything in Disney+, though, will be accomplished soon.

Also in the earnings report, Disney said that creator content will start appearing in the Disney+ app in December. This is related to the company’s deal with TikTok that debuted after its previous OpenAI deal fell apart when Sora was killed off. The Disney+ app will also get “more vertical video, live sports, and podcasts” soon too, Disney said.

title: Android Auto 18.2 update starts rolling out with more light mode teases
snippet: Google has started rolling out the Android Auto 18.2 update, but don’t expect much to change on your car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google has started rolling out the Android Auto 18.2 update, but don’t expect much to change on your car’s display.

Heading first to beta users, Android Auto 18.2 has started rolling out. This comes a little over a week after Android 18.1 hit the stable release track.

As Android Auto users should be very used to at this point, the update itself doesn’t bring any new user-facing changes that we can see. That’s not to say nothing is changing. There’s an endless list of bugs Google can fix. Just a few recent examples include Gemini bugs, foldable headaches, strange UI issues, connection problems, double-skipping songs, and more. Bug fixes are the primary point of these smaller Android Auto app updates.

Notably, this update also doesn’t fully cut off users on older Android versions yet. Google has confirmed Android 11 will be the new minimum requirement, but Android Auto 18.2 still supports as far back as Android 9.

	

Now, what about behind the scenes?

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Our teardown of Android Auto 18.2 didn’t turn up much of interest.

The biggest noteworthy change is that Google has updated over 100 assets within the Android Auto app in preparation of light mode support. These are largely around various button designs in the experience, such as:

res/drawable/ic_mr_button_connected_14_dark.xml

res/drawable/ic_mr_button_connected_15_dark.xml

Light mode for Android Auto is something we’ve been waiting ages to see go live, and every recent update has been building out the feature more and more. As for when it will be released, that’s anyone’s guess.

title: Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20
snippet: While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized. Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor. more…
fullText:
While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

Warby Parker

	

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Gentle Monster

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

The sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a new “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how big a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

There is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

When you’re capturing media that gets saved, there will always be a white blinking indicator light. There’s also another light in your field of vision that’s analogous to the camera and microphone privacy indicators in the top-right corner of Android phones. When I first put on the glasses, that light was distracting, but I quickly forgot about it by the end of my demo.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera. 

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands. 

Google built a number of privacy protections into Intelligent Eyewear that are clearly in response to the current perception of smart glasses. There are some interesting ideas here, starting with how Gemini queries that involve a picture (like a visual search) won’t be saved to your Gemini History, used for model training, or ad targeting. For example, if you ask Gemini to find out what kind of plant you’re looking at, that image won’t be accessible anywhere else. 

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.   

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

That indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place. 

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal issues. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

title: The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900
snippet: For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller. more…
fullText:
For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the company’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Buy Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 at lenovo.com

Buy Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 at bestbuy.com

Design and display

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

	

Still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

You might think an 8.8-inch display isn’t much of an upgrade over something like a Pixel 11 Pro XL, but aspect ratio is everything here.

Oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

Hardware, battery, and accessories

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually launched at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

If you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a big thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon shows that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Specs, software, and performance

Unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

We definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Big Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

DroidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

Now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

Obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

With all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

Scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app issues, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

It took three screenshots to capture the entire list.

You might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software update policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

Conclusion

I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just said, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

We have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

Lenovo’s Legion Tab Gen 5 is a powerful, mini gaming tablet, something you won’t find much of on store shelves these days. But with some software jank and a sky-high price, you might be better off waiting for a more powerful version — with OLED — in the months to come.

title: iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update
snippet: Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

Unlock with Front Camera feature 

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features come to iPhone Duo

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

title: iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates
snippet: iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

Apple Calendar moves key elements to bottom of screen in iOS 27.3, making them more reachable

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom. 

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

iOS 27.3 (left) vs iOS 27.2 (right)

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

title: Apple has renewed Slow Horses for seasons 7, 8, 9, and 10
snippet: Slow Horses isn’t going away anytime soon, as Apple TV confirmed today that the hit series has been renewed through season 10—meaning at least four more seasons are coming. more…
fullText:
Slow Horses isn’t going away anytime soon, as Apple TV confirmed today that the hit series has been renewed through season 10—meaning at least four more seasons are coming.

Slow Horses is getting at least four more seasons on Apple TV

The era of streaming TV has often been marked by shows being canceled too soon, and taking long breaks between seasons.

Slow Horses is a stark exception on both fronts. The British spy series premiered in 2022, and Apple TV recently finished airing its sixth season.

Apple has made a practice of ordering more Slow Horses seasons far sooner than most shows get renewed. Viewers now expect that at the end of one season, a trailer for the next season will debut.

But today Apple has extended Slow Horses far beyond what’s typical. Via Deadline, the company confirmed that Slow Horses has been renewed for seasons 9 and 10.

The latest approvals join the already-approved seasons 7 and 8.

	

It’s very rare for any show to run for 10 or more seasons. But it’s perhaps even harder to find a series that’s picked up for four additional seasons in advance.

Watch Slow Horses on Apple TV

Slow Horses season 6 wrapped up last month, and now fans know that there are at least four more seasons coming—likely with the same annual premiere cadence.

Are you a Slow Horses fan, and do you think the show could keep going on indefinitely? Let us know in the comments.
